source: Prelec, Seung, McCoy (2017) A solution to the single-question crowd wisdom problem, Nature 541:532-535
finding: Core idea: ask each person for their answer AND a prediction of how others will answer. Pick the answer whose actual share beats its average predicted share. Works because people who hold correct but rare knowledge know the majority is mistaken, so they predict a smaller share for their answer than naive voters predict for theirs.
numbers: Toy case: Philadelphia-is-capital question. Coin biases: yes 60% in actual world, 90% in counterfactual. Majority says yes in both worlds. Predicted yes share lies between 60% and 90%, actual converges to 60%, so no is surprisingly popular.
quote: selects the answer that gains more support than predicted
limits: Needs honest predictions; ideal-Bayesian proof only; infinite-sample guarantee.
agent_relevance: The scaffold would need a second elicitation (a prediction of other samples) per question, not just answers.

source: Prelec, Seung, McCoy (2017) A solution to the single-question crowd wisdom problem, Nature 541:532-535 - headline result
finding: Across seven studies and 490 binary items SP cut errors versus majority vote by 21.3%. On the 290 items with confidence, cuts were 35.8% vs majority, 24.2% vs confidence-weighted, 22.2% vs max-confidence.
numbers: 490 items, 21.3% (matched-pair sign test P<0.0005). 290 items: 35.8% (P<0.001), 24.2% (P=0.0107), 22.2% (P<0.13, not significant).
limits: Gain over max-confidence is not significant. Items pooled across studies of different size. Kappa highest for SP in every study (Fig 4), but per-study accuracy values only in figures.
agent_relevance: Effect is modest in absolute terms and driven by items where majority is wrong; the baseline here is human voters.

source: Prelec, Seung, McCoy (2017) A solution to the single-question crowd wisdom problem, Nature 541:532-535 - Studies 1a,b,c state capitals
finding: Studies 1a-c used 50 'X is the capital of Y' true/false items with three populations: 51 MIT Sloan MBA students (1a), 32 Princeton students (1b), 33 MIT BCS lab respondents (1c, with confidence). Majority fails on well-known confusions such as Philadelphia and Seattle.
numbers: 1a n=51, 1b n=32, 1c n=33; 50 items each. Across the three studies, voters for False predicted 49% would say True; voters for True predicted 73%.
limits: Small samples; students. Same item type three times, not independent domains.
agent_relevance: Famous-wrong-answer items are the best case for SP: a shared plausible error with a knowing minority.

source: Prelec, Seung, McCoy (2017) A solution to the single-question crowd wisdom problem, Nature 541:532-535 - Study 2 trivia
finding: Study 2: 80 true/false trivia questions (history, language, science, geography) from Sporcle, on Mechanical Turk, with confidence. Items were pre-piloted for varying percent correct.
numbers: 39 MTurk respondents, $5 flat fee, 80 items. False-voters predicted 45% would say true, true-voters predicted 59%. Spearman r between predicted vote share and own implied belief = 0.48.
limits: Tiny crowd (39). Pilot-selected items.
agent_relevance: The needed signal (minority knows it is a minority) is weaker in trivia than in state capitals.

source: Prelec, Seung, McCoy (2017) A solution to the single-question crowd wisdom problem, Nature 541:532-535 - Study 3 dermatology
finding: Study 3: 25 professional dermatologists (mean 10.5 years experience) judged 80 skin lesion images benign or malignant, with confidence and vote predictions. Two base-rate conditions (40 benign/20 malignant vs 20 benign/40 malignant).
numbers: 25 dermatologists (12 and 13 per condition), 80 items. Spearman r of predicted vote share with own belief = 0.87.
limits: Prediction was on an 11-point scale. Small expert panel.
agent_relevance: Expert domain with real stakes; SP kappa was highest here too.

source: Prelec, Seung, McCoy (2017) A solution to the single-question crowd wisdom problem, Nature 541:532-535 - Study 4 art prices
finding: Study 4: 90 20th century artworks; 20 MIT graduate students with no art training and a group of art professionals (mainly gallery managers) judged whether market price exceeds $30,000. Majority is biased toward the low category because shared base-rate knowledge is counted once per person.
numbers: 90 items. For a $100,000 artwork the average professional is right 30% of the time but a professional majority is directionally correct only 10% of the time. SP lowers the needed vote share for 'expensive' from 50% to about 25%.
quote: It is difficult for any expensive artwork to be recognized as such by a majority.
limits: Gallery-manager group size not given in main text. Four price bins collapsed to a binary.
agent_relevance: Clearest case of a double-counted prior: repeated samples share the same prior, so the majority amplifies bias.

source: Prelec, Seung, McCoy (2017) A solution to the single-question crowd wisdom problem, Nature 541:532-535 - impossibility of confidence
finding: Theorem 1: an infinite sample of correct posterior confidences is compatible with any answer being correct, so votes and confidences alone cannot identify truth even with ideal respondents. Fig. 2 gives identical confidence distributions for two coin problems with opposite correct answers.
numbers: Pure theory; counterexample with biased coins.
limits: Applies to ideal Bayesians who know priors and coin biases.
agent_relevance: Direct support for guardrail G4: more samples of the same kind of answer or confidence cannot fix a shared error.

source: Prelec, Seung, McCoy (2017) A solution to the single-question crowd wisdom problem, Nature 541:532-535 - Supplementary theory (Theorems 2 and 3)
finding: Model: m possible worlds (answers), n signals; respondents are Bayesian, signals iid given the world. Theorem 2: for binary questions the surprisingly popular answer is correct in the infinite-sample limit. Theorem 3 extends to multiple choice (m=n>2) using a Lemma that vote predictions identify respondents who put highest probability on the correct answer. Fully general m,n needs posteriors too.
numbers: Theory only. Needs each answer to have a unique signal that makes holders assign it highest probability.
limits: No finite-sample proof; ideal respondents assumed.
agent_relevance: For multi-answer questions the prediction must be a full distribution over answers, costly for free-form text.

source: Prelec, Seung, McCoy (2017) A solution to the single-question crowd wisdom problem, Nature 541:532-535 - simulation and power
finding: Simulated ideal Bayesian respondents: individuals correct 75%, majority 86% (the usual +11 points), SP nearly infallible with large samples. SP needs many questions to show significance.
numbers: 50 problems, n=30: SP beats majority at P<0.05 in only 40% of simulated studies (392 of 1000 in the SI power analysis). Sizes 6, 12, 33, 1000 simulated. A 90% majority is right about 90% of the time; a 55% majority is near chance.
limits: Simulation under uniform sampling of coin parameters.
agent_relevance: Gains are hard to detect with few items; plan evaluation with many items.

source: Prelec, Seung, McCoy (2017) A solution to the single-question crowd wisdom problem, Nature 541:532-535 - robustness and manipulation
finding: SP direction survives if respondents predict only for the world they think likelier, or if some give uninformative 50:50 predictions (result moves toward majority). A respondent can lie with a low prediction for a rival option; Bayesian truth serum scoring is suggested as a fix. Wording matters: ask 'given current evidence, is it more likely...'.
numbers: Share of predictions within 40-60%: 36% (states), 56% (trivia), 29% (art MIT), 19% (art professionals).
quote: do not guarantee success in practice, as actual respondents will fall short of ideal
limits: Authors admit claims are theoretical: actual respondents fall short of ideal. Works for factual questions, not preferences.
agent_relevance: If the agent samples do not predict each other, SP degrades to majority, in theory.

source: Wikipedia: Surprisingly popular
finding: Plain-language algorithm: ask a 'right' question (answer probability) and a 'popular' question (expected average answer by others). Choose the answer with the largest positive difference. Experts' two answers diverge; non-experts' cancel out. It avoids double counting of the shared prior.
numbers: Worked example: Philadelphia yes 65% vs predicted 75% (difference -10); no 35% vs predicted 25% (+10), so no wins.
limits: Encyclopedia summary, not a new test.
agent_relevance: Easy to implement in code: mean actual share minus mean predicted share per option.

source: Hosseini, Mandal, Shah, Shi (2021) Surprisingly Popular Voting Recovers Rankings, Surprisingly! (IJCAI)
finding: Extends SP to rankings. Prelec's version needs a prediction over all m! rankings. They elicit only top choice or full ranking for the vote, and top or ranking for the prediction (six formats), and convert ordinal predictions to cardinal ones with two tuned parameters.
numbers: 720 MTurk workers; geography (230 countries by population), movies (15,743 by box office), paintings (80 by auction price); 4 alternatives per question. A random ranking has Kendall-Tau distance 3; votes and predictions each land near 3 alone.
quote: even when the vote and prediction information are individually no better than random guesses
limits: Qualified workers only (90% approval, 100+ tasks, US East). Finite-sample theory left open.
agent_relevance: Even when votes and predictions are each near random, combining them beats classical voting rules; Rank-Rank beat all rules with a third of the samples. Richer predictions helped more than richer votes (Top-Rank beat Rank-Top).

source: Hosseini, Mandal, Puhan (2024) The Surprising Effectiveness of SP Voting with Partial Preferences
finding: Proposes Aggregated-SP and Partial-SP using votes and predictions over subsets of size k of m alternatives. Both beat Borda, Copeland, Maximin, Schulze; Partial-SP beats Aggregated-SP. Sample complexity depends on k and grows with k!.
numbers: 432 MTurk participants, 12 questions per domain, 36 alternatives per domain (countries, movies, paintings). Kendall-Tau and Spearman rho used.
limits: Schulze matches Aggregated-SP. Largest advantage in paintings, where expertise is specialised.
agent_relevance: SP-style scoring can run over pairwise or subset comparisons; useful when candidates are many.

source: Hosseini, Mandal, Puhan (2024) Surprisingly Popular Voting for Concentric Rank-Order Models
finding: Gives rank-order models (concentric Mallows, Plackett-Luce) under which SP voting provably recovers the ground-truth ranking, with sample complexity. On real data (432 participants) and simulation, SP voting beats Copeland and improves with sample size.
numbers: 432 participants, 12 questions each over three domains with 36 alternatives; simulated sample sizes varied.
limits: Needs a mixture with an informed minority group; model assumptions.
agent_relevance: Formal condition: SP helps only if an informed subgroup exists whose predictions differ from the naive group.

source: Hosseini, Mandal, Puhan (2025) SP-Rank: A Dataset for Ranked Preferences with Secondary Information
finding: Public dataset of over 12,000 human datapoints pairing a vote with a meta-prediction, across geography, movies, paintings and nine elicitation formats. SP-Voting beat Borda, Copeland, Maximin for full and subset rank recovery in 4- and 5-alternative settings. Authors suggest use for reward models in RLHF and DPO.
numbers: 12,000+ datapoints, 9 formats, 3 domains; Kendall-Tau tables.
limits: Same authors and similar MTurk tasks as earlier papers; not independent.
agent_relevance: A dataset to test an SP selector against real human second-order data.

source: Lee, Danileiko, Vi (2018) Testing the ability of the surprisingly popular method to predict NFL games, Judgment and Decision Making 13(4):322-333
finding: First test on a future event. SP applied to MTurk participants who rated themselves 'extremely knowledgeable' predicted 174 of 256 NFL 2017 games. It beat the mode of experts (172.5), the mode of media experts (172.5), confidence-weighted (166) and 87 of 94 media experts; five media experts were better.
numbers: 256 games, 100 MTurk participants, 94 media experts. SP 174 (68%) vs mode 172.5 vs confidence-weighted 166. Combining five methods reached 178.
limits: Self-selected 'extremely knowledgeable' subgroup chosen after the fact (exploratory). One season. Authors say results are 'exploratory, and need replication'. Media experts gave no meta-judgments. Rutchick et al. read it as SP not clearly better than the mode.
agent_relevance: Edge over the simple vote was about 1.5 games; weak evidence. A subgroup chosen after seeing data is a forking path.

source: Rutchick, Ross, Calvillo, Mesick (2020) Does the 'surprisingly popular' method yield accurate crowdsourced predictions? Cognitive Research 5:57 - Study 1 NFL
finding: Preregistered replication of Lee et al. with students. Whole sample: SP was worst. Top-quintile objective experts: SP best of the crowd methods but only narrowly; all crowd methods lost to fivethirtyeight and media.
numbers: N=227 students, 216 games (weeks 1-15, 2018). Individual 52.8%; democratic 53.9%; confidence-weighted 55.6%; SP 51.4%; fivethirtyeight 62.0%. Objective experts (46 people): democratic 59%, confidence-weighted 59.7%, SP 60.2% (130 games); media 65.0%. Only 6 self-rated 'extremely knowledgeable'.
limits: Student sample; part of season; differences of a few games, no reliable inference.
agent_relevance: SP gave no gain on a non-expert crowd; a partial failure to replicate.

source: Rutchick et al. (2020) - Study 2 midterm elections
finding: Predicting 110 races in the 2018 US midterms with 309 MTurk workers (92 of 401 excluded). Whole crowd: democratic 79.1% (87/110), SP about 80.0% (88). Self-rated experts (n=32): SP worst (71.8%, 79 races). Objective experts (62.5th percentile cut-off): SP best at 82.7% (91). fivethirtyeight 86.4% (95).
numbers: Individual 60.8%. 63-76 predictions per race. Made 5 days before the election. Table column order partly ambiguous in text extraction.
limits: Preregistered tests had very low sensitivity. Perfect scores (14/14) forced a looser expert cut-off.
agent_relevance: Self-rated expertise hurt SP; measured expertise helped. Choice of voting pool matters as much as the rule.

source: Rutchick et al. (2020) - Study 3 NBA
finding: Conceptual replication with NBA fans from Reddit (/r/NBA, /r/sportsbook) and a sport psychology class. This crowd was already expert. SP was the best crowd method.
numbers: N=130 (111 predicted); 465 games. Individual 61.8%; democratic 65.9% (306.5); confidence-weighted 65.5% (304.5); SP 67.3% (313); fivethirtyeight 68.2% (317). Quiz mean 12.6/19 vs students 3.39 and MTurk 3.73 (d about 2.3-2.5).
quote: Our samples come from one model and share its prior, the case SP targets, but there may be no informed minority.
limits: Gap of 6.5 games between SP and democratic; no strong test. Authors call overall findings inconclusive.
agent_relevance: SP edge appears only with a knowledgeable pool; SP still lost to a model-based forecaster.

source: Martinie, Wilkening, Howe (2020) Using meta-predictions to identify experts in the crowd when past performance is unknown, PLOS ONE 15(4):e0232058
finding: Meta-prediction weighting (MPW) uses forecasters' guesses about others to weight probabilistic forecasts. Extremised MPW beat simple average, pivoting, mean individual and others on 500 grade-school true/false science items at five difficulty levels.
numbers: 500 MTurk respondents, 100 trials each, 500 problems. Extremised MPW beat standard simple average by 6.64 points (95% CI 5.61-7.63), standard minimal pivoting by 4.21 (3.37-4.98), standard mean individual by 14.22. About 9 points over simple average on the hardest level.
limits: On an NCAA basketball dataset (Palley and Soll) with no experts, no significant difference among MPW, pivoting and simple average. SP is treated as a starting point, not tested head to head in this paper's results.
agent_relevance: Meta-prediction can serve as a continuous expert weight instead of a hard switch. Extremising conflicts with G4.

source: Wilkening, Martinie, Howe (2022) Hidden Experts in the Crowd, Management Science 68(1):487-508
finding: Confidence-based version of SP, robust to bias, weighting forecasters with more informative signals more heavily; reported to beat original SP on the same 500 problems.
numbers: Abstract-level only from search results; exact numbers not seen.
limits: Not opened; paywalled.
agent_relevance: Candidate refinement if basic SP shows promise.

source: Palley, Soll (2019) Extracting the wisdom of crowds when information is shared, Management Science 65(5):2291-2309
finding: Asks for own estimate plus predicted average of others; 'pivoting' removes the shared-information component and was reported to beat the simple average.
numbers: Abstract-level only; exact numbers not seen.
limits: Not opened; paywalled. Continuous estimates, not choices.
agent_relevance: Same logic as SP for numeric answers: shared prior counted repeatedly.

source: Prelec (2004) A Bayesian truth serum for subjective data, Science 306:462-466 (cited in Prelec et al. 2017)
finding: Precursor: respondents give an answer and predict the answer distribution; honest answers score by the log ratio of actual to predicted frequency, with truth-telling optimal. SP uses the same quantity as a truth signal.
numbers: Not read; described via Prelec et al. 2017 text: answers according to the log-ratio of actual to predicted votes.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: The log-ratio is a continuous version usable for ranking candidates.

source: Rutchick et al. (2020) - discussion of boundary conditions
finding: Authors conclude findings are inconclusive; with non-experts there is no evidence SP beats other methods, consistent with Lee et al. Prelec et al. found no systematic expertise effect but used non-experts successfully on factual items. Self-assessed expertise is unreliable.
numbers: Self-assessed expert counts: 6 of 227 (Study 1), 32 of 309 (Study 2), 18 predicting of 130 (Study 3).
limits: Prediction tasks differ from lookup facts; SP evidence on forecasts is thin and mixed.
agent_relevance: Test SP first on questions with a known single correct answer where a minority of samples knows it.

source: Prelec, Seung, McCoy (2017) A solution to the single-question crowd wisdom problem, Nature 541:532-535 - comparison with prediction markets and domain limits
finding: Authors contrast SP with prediction markets: both let experts overrule the majority, but SP accepts non-verifiable propositions and needs simple inputs. Limited to factual topics; result is the best answer in light of available evidence, not necessarily the truth.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Evidence may be incomplete or misleading.
agent_relevance: If the model lacks the fact in all samples, SP cannot find it.

source: Prelec, Seung, McCoy (2017) A solution to the single-question crowd wisdom problem, Nature 541:532-535 - confidence versus SP in practice
finding: In the state-capital example respondents voting for either answer are about equally confident (Fig. 1), so confidence weighting leaves the wrong majority in place while SP flips it.
numbers: SP vs confidence-weighted: 24.2% fewer errors, P=0.0107, on 290 items.
limits: Max-confidence comparison not significant (P<0.13).
agent_relevance: Self-reported confidence is not a substitute for a cross-prediction signal.

source: Hosseini et al. (2021) - effort of prediction versus vote
finding: Response time and perceived difficulty rise with richer formats; Top-Rank (simple vote, ranked prediction) beat Rank-Top at similar effort. A training step tunes two conversion parameters per format by grid search.
numbers: Six formats, 720 workers, 95% CIs on Kendall-Tau.
limits: Parameters fit on the same task type; risk of fitting to the domain.
agent_relevance: Spend the elicitation budget on the prediction side.

source: Hosseini et al. (2024) - concentric Mallows fit of crowd behaviour
finding: Data simulated from a concentric mixture of Mallows models reproduced the SP effect seen in human data: experts are a minority who vote near the truth and predict far from it; non-experts vote and predict far from the truth.
numbers: Real vs simulated Partial-SP with Copeland aggregation shows similar trends on pairwise and top-t hit rate (Fig 15).
limits: Model fit judged by parameter comparison, not a held-out test.
agent_relevance: Gives a testable model of when an informed minority exists.
